because i would like to open this up to questions and discussion as much as possible this is a really interesting time in indonesia with regards to human rights there are a lot of things going on some of them good a lot of them bad and the fact that we have a new government of president joko widodo

is a really unique opportunity to turn the page on what we at human rights watch have documented as a a very difficult 10-year regression in many key human rights indicators in indonesia under former president ezbaye but i want to start by giving credit where credit is due and the fact is is that over the past year there actually have been some improvements and some

advances in human rights in indonesia that need to be recognized and the first one is that i'd like to note that the indonesian government in july of 2014 passed a mental health law which is an important step toward addressing what is really a a silent and underreported mental health crisis in this country

this mental health law is not perfect but it's definitely a step in the right direction another issue i want to note is that [Music] president wadodo himself during his election campaign uh committed publicly to investigating uh specific instances of disappearances in 1998 this is a an important and symbolic step toward addressing

what has been decades of severe impunity for disappearances extrajudicial killings and other abuses by indonesia's security forces president widodo has made the commitment to investigate it investigate these disappearances we have yet to hear a precise plan and a precise timeline but it's still early days uh the other issue that's worth mentioning and this is related to uh

what i just mentioned is that over the past year uh there has been a loosening on the decades-long taboo about discussion and reporting on the 1965-1966 [Music] mass killings in indonesia human rights watch has publicly advocated with the indonesian government to open up its files to allow full disclosure and transparency about

those years and about those mass killings we're a long way from getting to that point but the fact that this topic which used to be completely taboo is now something that more people are feel more comfortable about discussing not least because of joshua oppenheimer's groundbreaking documentaries the act of killing and the

follow-up the look of silence which are widely available i believe through download here in indonesia so it's a step in the right direction and the final nod of recognition for improvement is that early in 2014 the indonesian government signed an agreement with the government of saudi arabia to help protect the rights of the many thousands of migrant workers from

indonesia who go to work in saudi arabia having said that indonesia's human rights challenges are considerable and president widodo is inheriting a legacy of worsening sectarian violence and intimidation against religious minorities there is ongoing security forces impunity particularly in papua and we are also seeing a very worrying

regression in women's rights in indonesia we see in indonesia and we have documented in this report which we released last year that religious minorities in indonesia are increasingly under attack they are under attack from militant islamists who have a strong sentiment of intolerance that lends itself to violence the targets are the ahmadiyya shia certain christian

communities and adding insult to injury of course is that elements of the indonesian government and the indonesian security forces are frequently passively or actively complicit in the harassment intimidation and violence against religious minorities in indonesia this is a key issue that the

government must confront sooner rather than later president yudhoyono absolutely failed to address this issue so it now lands in the inbox of president widodo the other issue i want to mention that's related to that is we have noted how sharia law and ace has serious implications for human rights we saw

late last year that the aceh provincial government passed two bylaws that outlawed same-sex relations as well as any sexual relations outside of marriage the punishment for those transgressions being uh up to 100 lashes as law along with fines and imprisonment these developments are seriously worrying in terms of the implications for the human rights environment

for the people of aceh and this is something that we are continuing to engage with the indonesian government on final issue i want to talk about really quickly is the issue of women's rights i think probably the most emblematic indicator of the regression in women's rights in indonesia and the government's tolerance of attacks on women's rights in
